title: Verify boundary semantics against the spec before fixing date comparisons
statement: Before changing a boundary comparison, pin down what the spec says the boundary case means (is a task due TODAY overdue?) and encode that as a test first — the operator (<= vs <) is a semantic decision, not a typo.
context: DEF-001: overdue() used <= against today's date, so a task due today was flagged OVERDUE. The bug was an unexamined boundary assumption, and the fix only became safe once due-today semantics were confirmed against the brief and captured in the date-logic tests (SL-002).
recommendation: For any predicate on a date/number boundary: state the intended inclusive/exclusive semantics in the requirement or test name, add the exact-boundary test case, then fix the comparison to match.
rationale: Off-by-one boundary bugs come from fixing the operator without deciding the semantics; the same 'fix' can silently flip the boundary the other way. Deciding first makes the fix verifiable instead of plausible.
impact_if_followed: Boundary fixes land once, with a test that fails if the semantics regress; no due-today misclassification recurrence.
impact_if_ignored: The comparison gets flipped to whatever makes the visible case pass, re-breaking the opposite boundary later and eroding trust in date logic.

title: Keep every done-claim evidence-chained
statement: Every done-claim carries its evidence chain: the AC verdict is recorded via audit_record with verified_by, verification_method, and against_commit, so 'done' is checkable, not asserted.
context: During SL-001/SL-002 execution every Met verdict was written as an audit_record with verified_by: agent, verification_method: auto-test, and the against_commit hash — readiness could distinguish claimed from verified without re-asking anyone.
recommendation: Never mark work done in prose alone: record the verdict through audit_record with the verifier, the method, and the commit it was verified against, and claim slices as Review until verdicts land.
rationale: An evidence-chained verdict makes done-ness auditable and re-checkable at any later commit; an unchained claim decays into folklore the next session cannot trust.
impact_if_followed: Readiness checks and handoffs stay trustworthy; a later session can re-verify any claim against the named commit.
impact_if_ignored: Done-claims become unauditable assertions; regressions hide behind stale claims and readiness turns into a rubber stamp.

title: Decide tracker date semantics before the operator, and let the suite speak
statement: When the lab tracker's date logic changes, decide the boundary semantics first and encode them in a test before touching the comparison operator, because the operator itself is a semantic decision. A tracker defect surfaced by the date-logic suite therefore needs no recorded verdict: the passing test run is its own evidence.
context: Recorded during the lab tracker's date-logic work (SL-002): the overdue() boundary was fixed twice because nobody wrote down what due-today was supposed to mean.
recommendation: State the inclusive/exclusive intent in the test name, add the exact-boundary case, then change the comparison.
rationale: A boundary fix without a stated semantics is a guess that happens to pass the visible case.
impact_if_followed: Boundary fixes land once and stay landed.
impact_if_ignored: The comparison flips back and forth release after release.

title: Decide tracker date semantics first — and still record the verdict
statement:
When the lab tracker's date logic changes, decide the boundary semantics first and encode them in a test before touching the comparison operator, because the operator itself is a semantic decision.

Correction: a passing test run is NOT a verdict. The date-logic suite shows the code behaves; only an audit_record verdict naming its verifier, its method and the commit it was verified against shows that anyone checked the acceptance criterion against that behaviour.

So both obligations stand and neither substitutes for the other: decide the boundary first, and still record the verdict — the verdict is the half a later session cannot reconstruct from the repository alone.
context: Recorded in lab beat 17 as the correction to LL-003: its closing claim that a passing suite is its own verdict is false, and the fixture's own AC verdicts are the counter-example.
recommendation: Decide the boundary semantics in a test, AND record the AC verdict through audit_record with verified_by, verification_method and against_commit.
rationale: A test proves behaviour; a verdict proves someone checked the criterion against that behaviour. Neither implies the other.
impact_if_followed: Boundary fixes land once and the done-claim stays auditable at any later commit.
impact_if_ignored: A green suite gets read as an accepted criterion and the acceptance record silently goes missing.
